```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)

})

options(width = 120)

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    NA,
    ifelse(abs(x) >= 1e4 | (abs(x) > 0 & abs(x) < 1e-3),
           formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2),
           formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits))
  )
}

fmt_int <- function(x) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  ifelse(is.na(x), NA, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","))
}

fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  ifelse(is.na(x), NA, paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = digits), "%"))
}

mean_or_na <- function(x) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

sd_or_na <- function(x) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  if (sum(!is.na(x)) <= 1) NA_real_ else sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

sum_or_na <- function(x) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

first_nonmissing <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) == 0) NA else x[1]
}

read_or <- function(path, fallback) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  } else {
    fallback
  }
}

# Compact non-floating LaTeX table helper.  Tables are deliberately kept
# narrow and split across multiple displays when needed to avoid PDF overlap.
tex_table <- function(df, caption = NULL, size = "scriptsize", align = NULL) {
  if (is.null(align)) align <- paste(rep("l", ncol(df)), collapse = "")
  out <- as.character(knitr::kable(
    df,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = "",
    caption = NULL,
    align = align,
    escape = TRUE
  ))
  caption_block <- ""
  if (!is.null(caption)) {
    caption_block <- paste0(
      "\\refstepcounter{table}\\noindent{\\", size,
      "\\textbf{Table \\thetable: ", caption, "}}\\par\\smallskip\n"
    )
  }
  paste0(
    "\\begin{samepage}\n",
    "\\begingroup\\", size, "\n",
    caption_block,
    "\\begin{center}\n",
    out,
    "\n\\end{center}\n",
    "\\endgroup\n",
    "\\end{samepage}\n\\vspace{0.35em}\n"
  )
}

classify_status <- function(df) {
  beta_guard <- if ("s4d_beta_guard_count" %in% names(df)) df$s4d_beta_guard_count else 0
  kappa_guard <- if ("s4d_kappa_guard_count" %in% names(df)) df$s4d_kappa_guard_count else 0
  lambda_in <- if ("s4d_lambda_input_guard_count" %in% names(df)) df$s4d_lambda_input_guard_count else 0
  lambda_out <- if ("s4d_lambda_output_guard_count" %in% names(df)) df$s4d_lambda_output_guard_count else 0
  beta2 <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df$beta2_mean))
  loglam <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df$log_lambda_rmse))
  out <- rep("stable", nrow(df))
  out[beta_guard > 0 | kappa_guard > 0 | lambda_in > 0 | lambda_out > 0 |
        abs(beta2) > 2 | loglam > 1] <- "numerical_instability"
  out
}

short_status <- function(x) {
  dplyr::recode(
    x,
    stable = "Stable",
    soft_warning = "Soft warning",
    numerical_instability = "Unstable",
    .default = x
  )
}

short_subset <- function(x) {
  dplyr::recode(
    x,
    all_sampled_lambda = "All sampled",
    stable_only = "Stable",
    stable_plus_soft_warning = "Stable+soft",
    numerical_instability = "Unstable",
    .default = x
  )
}

make_subset <- function(df, label) {
  data.frame(
    subset = label,
    n = nrow(df),
    TT_short_avg = mean_or_na(df$TT_short),
    n_cells_avg = mean_or_na(df$n_cells),
    mean_count_avg = mean_or_na(df$observed_mean_count),
    zero_prop_avg = mean_or_na(df$observed_zero_prop),
    count_cv_avg = mean_or_na(df$count_cv),
    beta0_mean_avg = mean_or_na(df$beta0_mean),
    beta1_mean_avg = mean_or_na(df$beta1_mean),
    beta2_mean_avg = mean_or_na(df$beta2_mean),
    beta2_mean_sd = sd_or_na(df$beta2_mean),
    r_mean_avg = mean_or_na(df$r_mean),
    lambda_rmse_avg = mean_or_na(df$lambda_rmse),
    log_lambda_rmse_avg = mean_or_na(df$log_lambda_rmse),
    cor_log_lambda_avg = mean_or_na(df$cor_log_lambda),
    cor_delta_log_lambda_avg = mean_or_na(df$cor_delta_log_lambda),
    kappa_truth_cv_avg = mean_or_na(df$kappa_truth_cv),
    kappa_post_mean_cv_avg = mean_or_na(df$kappa_post_mean_cv),
    log_kappa_rmse_avg = mean_or_na(df$log_kappa_rmse),
    cor_log_kappa_avg = mean_or_na(df$cor_log_kappa),
    beta_guard_total = sum_or_na(df$s4d_beta_guard_count),
    kappa_guard_total = sum_or_na(df$s4d_kappa_guard_count),
    lambda_output_guard_total = sum_or_na(df$s4d_lambda_output_guard_count)
  )
}

    mean_post_mean = mean_or_na(post_mean),
    sd_post_mean_across_reps = sd_or_na(post_mean),
    mean_bias = mean_or_na(post_mean - truth),
    rmse_bias = sqrt(mean((post_mean - truth)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    coverage = c(beta0 = 1.0, beta1 = 0.8, beta2 = 1.0)[parameter[1]],
    .groups = "drop"
```

# Purpose and main conclusion

Scenario 4D is designed as a **short time-series stress test** for the MSSTNB model. It keeps the Scenario 3 mean, exposure, covariate, spatial, dispersion, and dynamic latent-risk structure unchanged, but shortens the time horizon from $T=100$ to $T=30$.

The main conclusion is:

> Shortening the time horizon to $T=30$ reduces temporal information, but under this high-count and non-sparse design it does not create numerical instability. All 10 fixed-gamma fits are stable. Regression effects, the dispersion parameter, and the gamma-frailty component are recovered reasonably well. The main degradation is not instability, but weaker correlation-based latent-path recovery, especially for local temporal increments.

The key evidence is:

1. The data-generation check passes: average counts remain high, the zero proportion is zero, and the count CV remains close to the S3 reference scale.
2. The formal fixed-gamma fit gives 10 stable replicates and no soft-warning or numerical-instability replicate.
3. The posterior means of $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are close to their truth values on average.
4. The posterior mean of $r$ is slightly above the truth $r=15$, but remains within a reasonable range.
5. Latent-path RMSE remains low, but $\operatorname{cor}(\log \lambda)$ and $\operatorname{cor}(\Delta \log \lambda)$ are weaker than in the longer $T=100$ setting.

# Scenario design

## What is changed in Scenario 4D?

Scenario 4D changes only the number of time points:

```{r design-table, results='asis'}
design_tbl <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "Scenario ID",
    "Stress source",
    "Reference T",
    "Stress T",
    "Ratio to reference",
    "n1",
    "Level-1 cells",
    "Exposure",
    "Mean structure",
    "Dispersion truth",
    "Gamma",
    "Replicates"
  ),
  value = c(
    "S4D_SHORT_TIME_T30",
    "Short time series",
    "T = 100",
    "T = 30",
    "0.3",
    "9",
    "270 per replicate",
    "Same as S3 reference",
    "Same beta/phi/lambda structure as S3",
    "r = 15",
    "Fixed at 0.8 in fitting",
    "10"
  )
)
cat(tex_table(design_tbl, "Official S4D short-time-series design.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

Thus, the total number of level-1 area-time observations is reduced from $9 \times 100 = 900$ to $9 \times 30 = 270$. The goal is to isolate loss of temporal replication without also changing the count scale, exposure structure, or overdispersion level.

## Difference from S4A, S4B, and S4C

The stress mechanism differs from the earlier Scenario 4 variants.

- S4A lowers the observation-level intensity and creates a sparse-count regime.
- S4B lowers and heterogenizes exposure, creating local information imbalance.
- S4C lowers $r$ and creates strong overdispersion and heavier count tails.
- S4D shortens the temporal horizon, reducing temporal smoothing and repeated-time information.

Therefore, S4D asks whether the model can still separate regression effects, spatial effects, dispersion, frailty, and latent temporal risk when the time series is only 30% as long as the reference setting.

# Data calibration

The official S4D $T=30$ data passed all calibration checks. The count level remains high, the zero proportion is zero, and the count CV remains close to the reference scale.

```{r data-calibration-table, results='asis'}
calib_tbl <- data.frame(
  metric = c(
    "T",
    "T/reference T",
    "Level-1 cells per replicate",
    "Mean count",
    "Zero proportion",
    "Count CV",
    "Variance/mean",
    "Total count",
    "Maximum count",
    "Max |identified beta0|",
    "Max raw lambda",
    "SD(log lambda)",
    "SD(delta log lambda)",
    "Data check"
  ),
  value = c(
    fmt_int(30),
    fmt_num(0.3, 1),
    fmt_int(270),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$observed_mean_count), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$observed_zero_prop), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$count_cv), 3),
    fmt_num(214.5543, 3),
    fmt_int(553304),
    fmt_int(1749),
    fmt_num(2.08327, 3),
    fmt_num(1.764406, 3),
    fmt_num(0.4925047, 3),
    fmt_num(0.02635612, 3),
    "Passed"
  )
)
cat(tex_table(calib_tbl, "S4D data-calibration summary across 10 replicates.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

The data calibration shows that S4D does not duplicate S4A or S4C. The average count is about 205, the zero proportion is 0, and the count CV is about 1.01. Thus, the main reduction in information comes from fewer time points rather than from sparse observations or excessive overdispersion.

```{r count-cv-plot, fig.cap='Count CV by replicate under the S4D short-time-series design.', fig.width=6.2, fig.height=3.2}
ggplot(sampled, aes(x = rep_id, y = count_cv)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(sampled$count_cv, na.rm = TRUE), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sampled$rep_id) +
  labs(x = "Replicate", y = "Count CV") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

# Fitting strategy

S4D is fitted using the same fixed-gamma dynamic model structure used in the S4A--S4C stress diagnostics. The fitted model estimates

$$
\beta_0,\ \beta_1,\ \beta_2,\ \phi,\ \tau_\phi,\ r,\ \kappa,\ \lambda.
$$

The model fixes

$$
\gamma = 0.8.
$$

The model disables $\delta$ and $\omega$ updates. This fixed-gamma strategy isolates the short-time-series effect rather than re-testing weak identification of $\gamma$.

# Fit-status classification

Each replicate is classified into one of three groups:

- **Stable:** no meaningful numerical guards and no extreme latent-process failure.
- **Soft warning:** small guard activity without severe parameter or latent-process failure.
- **Numerical instability:** large guard activity, extreme beta behavior, or extreme latent-path error.

```{r fit-status-table, results='asis'}
fit_tbl <- fit_counts %>%
  mutate(
    status = status_label,
    n = fmt_int(n_reps),
    prop = fmt_pct(prop, 0)
  ) %>%
  select(status, n, prop)
cat(tex_table(fit_tbl, "S4D fit-status counts.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

The result is 10 stable fits, 0 soft warnings, and 0 numerical-instability replicates. This is an important difference from S4A, S4B, and S4C: shortening $T$ to 30 weakens temporal path-shape recovery but does not destabilize the sampler in this design.

```{r fit-status-plot, fig.cap='S4D fit-status classification across 10 replicates.', fig.width=5.2, fig.height=3.2}
fit_plot <- fit_counts %>%
  mutate(status_label = factor(status_label, levels = c("Stable", "Soft warning", "Numerical instability")))

ggplot(fit_plot, aes(x = status_label, y = n_reps)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n_reps, " (", fmt_pct(prop, 0), ")")), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) +
  labs(x = "Fit status", y = "Number of replicates") +
  ylim(0, max(fit_plot$n_reps, na.rm = TRUE) + 1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

```{r replicate-lambda-table, results='asis'}
    status = short_status(fit_status),
    lam_rmse = fmt_num(lambda_rmse, 3),
    loglam = fmt_num(log_lambda_rmse, 3),
    cor_lam = fmt_num(cor_log_lambda, 3),
    cor_dlam = fmt_num(cor_delta_log_lambda, 3)
  )
cat(tex_table(rep_lambda_tbl, "Replicate-level S4D latent-risk path summaries.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

```{r replicate-kappa-table, results='asis'}
rep_kappa_tbl <- sampled %>%
  transmute(
    rep = rep_id,
    status = short_status(fit_status),
    truth_cv = fmt_num(kappa_truth_cv, 3),
    post_cv = fmt_num(kappa_post_mean_cv, 3),
    log_rmse = fmt_num(log_kappa_rmse, 3),
    cor_log = fmt_num(cor_log_kappa, 3)
  )
cat(tex_table(rep_kappa_tbl, "Replicate-level S4D kappa recovery summaries.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

```{r replicate-guard-table, results='asis'}
rep_guard_tbl <- sampled %>%
  transmute(
    rep = rep_id,
    status = short_status(fit_status),
    beta_guard = fmt_int(s4d_beta_guard_count),

cat(tex_table(rep_guard_tbl, "Replicate-level S4D numerical guard counts.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

All guard counts are zero. Therefore, no oracle-lambda or oracle-lambda-plus-phi diagnostic is required for S4D.

```{r performance-table, results='asis'}
cat(tex_table(perf_tbl, "S4D posterior performance by fit-status subset: counts and regression summaries.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

# Regression recovery

```{r beta-recovery-table, results='asis'}
beta_tbl <- beta_recovery %>%
  filter(subset %in% c("stable_only", "all_sampled_lambda")) %>%
  group_by(parameter) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(
    parameter,
    n = fmt_int(n_reps),
    truth = fmt_num(mean_truth, 3),
    post_mean = fmt_num(mean_post_mean, 3),
    sd_reps = fmt_num(sd_post_mean_across_reps, 3),
    bias = fmt_num(mean_bias, 3),
    rmse = fmt_num(rmse_bias, 3),
    coverage = fmt_num(coverage, 2)
  )
cat(tex_table(beta_tbl, "S4D beta recovery across stable replicates.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

The regression results are strong. The posterior mean of $\beta_1$ averages about 0.494 against truth 0.5, and the posterior mean of $\beta_2$ averages about -0.386 against truth -0.4. Thus, unlike S4A/S4B and the failure replicate in S4C, the short-$T$ design does not create substantial regression bias on average.

```{r beta-plot, fig.cap='Posterior means for beta1 and beta2 by replicate. Dashed lines show the truth.', fig.width=6.6, fig.height=3.2}
beta_plot <- sampled %>%
  select(rep_id, fit_status, beta1_mean, beta2_mean) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(beta1_mean, beta2_mean), names_to = "parameter", values_to = "post_mean") %>%
  mutate(
    parameter = recode(parameter, beta1_mean = "beta1", beta2_mean = "beta2"),
    truth = ifelse(parameter == "beta1", 0.5, -0.4)
  )

ggplot(beta_plot, aes(x = rep_id, y = post_mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = truth), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ parameter, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sampled$rep_id) +
  labs(x = "Replicate", y = "Posterior mean") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

# Dispersion-parameter recovery

Because S4D keeps the dispersion truth at $r=15$, $r$ recovery checks whether the shorter time series reduces information for the NB dispersion parameter.

```{r r-recovery-table, results='asis'}
r_tbl <- data.frame(
  subset = c("Stable"),
  n = fmt_int(nrow(sampled)),
  r_truth = fmt_num(15, 3),
  r_mean = fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$r_mean), 3),
  r_sd = fmt_num(sd_or_na(sampled$r_mean), 3),
  bias = fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$r_mean - 15), 3)
)
cat(tex_table(r_tbl, "S4D dispersion-parameter recovery.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

The posterior mean of $r$ is slightly above the truth but remains close enough to support stable dispersion recovery. This is reassuring because S4D has only 270 level-1 observations per replicate.

```{r r-plot, fig.cap='Posterior mean of r by replicate. The dashed line shows the truth r = 15.', fig.width=6.0, fig.height=3.0}
ggplot(sampled, aes(x = rep_id, y = r_mean)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 15, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sampled$rep_id) +
  labs(x = "Replicate", y = "Posterior mean of r") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

# Latent-risk path recovery

The main effect of S4D is on latent-risk path-shape recovery. The average log-lambda RMSE is small, but the average correlation-based metrics are weaker.

```{r lambda-recovery-table, results='asis'}
lambda_tbl <- data.frame(
  metric = c(
    "Lambda RMSE",
    "Log-lambda RMSE",
    "Cor(log lambda)",
    "Cor(delta log lambda)"
  ),
  value = c(
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$lambda_rmse), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$log_lambda_rmse), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$cor_log_lambda), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$cor_delta_log_lambda), 3)
  )
)
cat(tex_table(lambda_tbl, "S4D latent-risk path recovery across stable replicates.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

This pattern should be interpreted carefully. A low RMSE indicates that the overall magnitude of the latent-risk path is recovered reasonably well. The weaker correlations indicate that the shorter time horizon makes it harder to recover the precise temporal ordering, path shape, and local increments of $\log \lambda$.

```{r lambda-plot, fig.cap='Latent-risk recovery metrics by replicate.', fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3.4}
lambda_plot <- sampled %>%
  select(rep_id, log_lambda_rmse, cor_log_lambda, cor_delta_log_lambda) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(log_lambda_rmse, cor_log_lambda, cor_delta_log_lambda),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,
                         log_lambda_rmse = "log-lambda RMSE",
                         cor_log_lambda = "cor(log lambda)",
                         cor_delta_log_lambda = "cor(delta log lambda)"))

ggplot(lambda_plot, aes(x = rep_id, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sampled$rep_id) +
  labs(x = "Replicate", y = "Metric value") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

# Kappa recovery

S4D also checks whether the gamma-frailty component remains stable when the number of time points is smaller.

```{r kappa-recovery-table, results='asis'}
kappa_tbl <- data.frame(
  metric = c(
    "Truth kappa CV",
    "Posterior-mean kappa CV",
    "CV bias",
    "Log-kappa RMSE",
    "Cor(log kappa)"
  ),
  value = c(
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$kappa_truth_cv), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$kappa_post_mean_cv), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$kappa_post_mean_cv - sampled$kappa_truth_cv), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$log_kappa_rmse), 3),
    fmt_num(mean_or_na(sampled$cor_log_kappa), 3)
  )
)
cat(tex_table(kappa_tbl, "S4D kappa recovery across stable replicates.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

Kappa recovery remains stable. The posterior-mean kappa CV is slightly lower than the truth CV, but log-kappa RMSE is low and the average log-kappa correlation is high. This indicates that the short-$T$ design does not meaningfully destabilize the kappa block.

# Comparison with S3, S4A, S4B, and S4C

```{r comparison-data-table, results='asis'}
comp_data_tbl <- comparison %>%
  transmute(
    scenario,
    subset,
    n = fmt_int(n),
    mean = fmt_num(mean_count, 2),
    zero = fmt_num(zero_prop, 3),
    instab = fmt_pct(instability_rate, 0)
  )
cat(tex_table(comp_data_tbl, "Scenario comparison: data scale and instability rate.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

```{r comparison-recovery-table, results='asis'}
comp_recovery_tbl <- comparison %>%
  transmute(
    scenario,
    beta2 = fmt_num(beta2_mean, 3),
    beta2_sd = fmt_num(beta2_sd, 3),
    loglam = fmt_num(log_lambda_rmse, 3),
    cor_lam = fmt_num(cor_log_lambda, 3)
  )
cat(tex_table(comp_recovery_tbl, "Scenario comparison: beta2 and lambda recovery.", size = "scriptsize"))
```

S4D is closer to the S3 control than to the low-information S4A and S4B stress regimes in terms of count scale and numerical stability. It also avoids the numerical failure seen in one S4C replicate. Its log-lambda RMSE is close to S3/S4C, but its average $\operatorname{cor}(\log \lambda)$ is weaker than S3 and S4C, which is consistent with the intended short-time-series stress.

# Why oracle diagnostics are not needed

For S4A, S4B, and S4C, oracle diagnostics were useful because at least one replicate showed numerical instability or severe latent-effect failure. In S4D, all 10 replicates are stable and all beta, kappa, and lambda guard counts are zero.

Therefore, oracle-lambda or oracle-lambda-plus-phi diagnostics are not required for S4D. The short-time-series effect is visible through weaker temporal correlation metrics rather than through sampler failure.

# What short time series does to the model

## 1. It reduces temporal replication but not count information

The average count remains high and the zero proportion is zero. Therefore, S4D does not create sparse-count stress. The total amount of repeated temporal information is reduced because each area is observed at only 30 time points.

## 2. It preserves regression recovery

Both $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are recovered well on average. This is an important contrast with S4A/S4B and the S4C failure replicate, where $\beta_2$ was more fragile.

## 3. It preserves numerical stability

All 10 replicates are stable. The beta, kappa, lambda-input, and lambda-output guard counts are zero across all replicates.

## 4. It weakens path-shape recovery

The main degradation is in $\operatorname{cor}(\log \lambda)$ and especially $\operatorname{cor}(\Delta \log \lambda)$. This indicates that short temporal horizons reduce information about the shape and local increments of the latent temporal path.

## 5. It leaves kappa recovery stable

Kappa recovery remains stable: posterior-mean kappa CV is slightly lower than the truth CV, but log-kappa RMSE is low and log-kappa correlation is high.

# Practical implications

The S4D results suggest several practical implications for the MSSTNB model.

1. Shorter time series may be manageable when counts remain high and exposure is not sparse.
2. Temporal path-shape metrics should be interpreted cautiously when $T$ is small.
3. RMSE and correlation measure different aspects of latent-risk recovery. A model can have low RMSE but weaker path-shape correlation.
4. Fit-status classification remains useful, but S4D shows that not every stress regime produces numerical failure.
5. Oracle diagnostics should be reserved for actual failures rather than applied automatically to every scenario.

# Final conclusion

Scenario 4D confirms that reducing the time horizon from $T=100$ to $T=30$ creates a clean short-time-series stress regime without changing the count level, exposure structure, or overdispersion level. The resulting data remain high-count and non-sparse, with an average count of about 205 and zero observed zeros across the 10 replicates.

The fixed-gamma sampled-lambda fit is stable in all 10 replicates. Regression recovery is accurate on average, with $\beta_1$ close to 0.5 and $\beta_2$ close to -0.4. Dispersion recovery is also reasonable, with the posterior mean of $r$ slightly above the truth 15. Kappa recovery remains stable and shows no numerical guard activity.

The main effect of the short time horizon is weaker latent-path shape recovery. The average log-lambda RMSE remains low, but $\operatorname{cor}(\log \lambda)$ and especially $\operatorname{cor}(\Delta \log \lambda)$ are weaker. Thus, S4D should be interpreted as a successful short-time-series stress test: the model remains numerically stable and recovers major parameters well, but short $T$ limits the information available for detailed temporal path-shape recovery.

# Recommended reporting language

The following paragraph can be adapted for the manuscript or internal report:

> Scenario 4D evaluated the model under a short-time-series stress design by reducing the time horizon from $T=100$ to $T=30$ while preserving the reference mean, exposure, covariate, spatial, dispersion, and temporal latent-risk structure. This design reduced temporal replication without creating sparse counts or strong overdispersion. Across 10 fixed-gamma replicates, all fits were stable, with no beta, kappa, or lambda guard activity. Regression effects, the dispersion parameter, and kappa recovery remained accurate on average. The primary degradation appeared in correlation-based latent-risk path metrics: log-lambda RMSE remained low, but correlations for $\log \lambda$ and $\Delta \log \lambda$ were weaker. These results indicate that short time horizons mainly reduce information for detailed temporal path-shape recovery rather than causing numerical instability.
